standard.title: Text stages and phases
standard.description: Describe how spoken, written and multimodal texts use language features and are typically organised into characteristic stages and phases, depending on purposes in texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify how texts across the curriculum have different language features and are organised for different purposes, and identify some characteristic stages (AC9E4LA03). They have not yet described the internal phase structure within stages, or compared how the same genre adapts across spoken, written and multimodal modes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the characteristic stages and phases of a range of text types — including narrative, procedure, argument, explanation, discussion and information report — explaining how language features within each stage serve the text's purpose, and how these structures adapt across spoken, written and multimodal modes.

nodes.label: Stages serve purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the characteristic stages of familiar text types and explain how each stage contributes to the text's overall purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and label the stages of at least two text types (e.g. narrative, information report) and explain what communicative work each stage does.
nodes.typical_width: Map stages across a range of text types including narrative, procedure, argument, explanation, and information report. For each, explain how the sequence of stages builds toward the text's purpose, and why stages are ordered as they are.
wider: Compare how the same text type (e.g. argument) is staged differently across spoken, written and multimodal forms, and explain what the structural differences reveal about audience and context
Examine texts where conventional stage ordering is disrupted (e.g. in medias res narrative, or delayed thesis argument) and discuss the effect of that disruption
nodes.hinge_reason: Stage identification and purpose-function explanation is prerequisite for Node 2's phase analysis and Node 3's language-feature mapping. Students who cannot identify and explain stages cannot locate phases within them, and cannot reason about why particular language features cluster in particular structural positions.

response_modes.reason: Stage identification across multiple text types requires practice to become reliable. Students who have mapped only narrative stages will apply narrative assumptions to argument or explanation text structures. Consolidation through deliberate practice across text types builds the cross-genre stage recognition that Node 2 and Node 3 depend on.

success_criteria: Labels the stages of a given text type correctly and explains the communicative function of each stage.
Explains why removing or reordering a stage would disrupt the text's purpose.

nodes.label: Phases within stages
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify phases within stages and explain how phases build the communicative work of the stage they belong to.
nodes.minimum_width: In a text with identifiable stages, identify at least one stage and describe its internal phases — how the stage unfolds through a sequence of smaller moves.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the phase structure of multiple stages across at least two text types, explaining how phases sequence within stages and what language features signal phase transitions (e.g. paragraph openers, sentence starters, cohesive devices).
wider: Compare how paragraphs function as phase units differently in narrative, argument, and procedural recount texts — examining how topic sentence position and function shifts across text types
Examine how phases are signalled visually in multimodal texts (layout, headings, images) versus through language in written texts
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to explain language features characteristic of specific stages and phases. Students who cannot distinguish a phase from a paragraph or a stage cannot locate language features within their structural position, and therefore cannot explain why those features appear where they do.

response_modes.reason: The distinction between a stage and a phase — and what makes something a phase rather than just a sentence — requires explicit scaffolding. Students need a reasoning framework: 'What job is this paragraph doing? Is that job the whole stage's job, or part of it?' without this, students conflate paragraph with phase.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one stage and describes two or more phases within it, explaining what communicative work each phase does.
Identifies a language feature (sentence opener, connective, paragraph structure) that signals a phase transition.

nodes.label: Language features signal structure
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify specific language features used in different stages and phases, and explain how those features serve the communicative purpose of that structural position.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two language features characteristic of a specific stage or phase in a text type, and explain why those features are suited to the stage's purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the characteristic language features of stages across narrative, argument, explanation, discussion and information report texts. Explain how language choices are constrained by stage function — why certain verb tenses, clause types, or vocabulary fields cluster in particular stages.
wider: Compare how language features in equivalent stages differ across spoken, written and multimodal realisations of the same text type
Examine how writers deliberately violate expected language features for effect (e.g. using present tense in historical recount) and explain what effect the violation creates

response_modes.reason: The range of text types and the language feature patterns associated with their stages is a knowledge base students need to accumulate. Students who have only analysed narrative stages will struggle when encountering explanation or discussion text structures. Breadth across text types is the target at this node.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The full range of text types in the elaborations — narrative, procedure, argument, explanation, discussion, information report, historical recount, procedural recount, review, poem — provides genuine richness. Advancing students can build a systematic map of language feature patterns across multiple text types, which is substantive analytical work within year band.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two specific language features (e.g. relational verbs in information reports, action verbs in procedures) and explains why they appear in that stage.
Explains the relationship between a language feature and the stage it appears in — not just names the feature.

nodes.label: Describing texts across modes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how the same genre structures adapt across spoken, written and multimodal modes, identifying what changes and what remains consistent.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare one text type realised in at least two modes (e.g. written argument and spoken argument) and describe at least two structural or language feature differences, explaining why the mode affects those features.
nodes.typical_width: Describe how genre structures and language features adapt across spoken, written, digital and multimodal forms for at least two text types. Explain what the constraints of each mode do to stage structure, phase organisation, and language feature choices.
wider: Analyse a digital or multimedia text that blends multiple genres (e.g. a documentary that combines information report and recount) and describe how stage structures from different genres are interwoven

Compare how narrative, argument and explanation texts are structured differently when composed in digital mind map, linear written, or spoken presentation form — discussing what the compositional medium makes possible or constrains

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to apply stage/phase knowledge (nodes 1–2) and language feature knowledge (node 3) simultaneously to texts across modes. The integration — tracking both structural and language feature shifts across modes — is the full demand of the descriptor.

success_criteria: Describes at least two differences in structure or language features when comparing the same text type across two modes.
Explains why at least one of those differences is a consequence of the mode (not just describes that it exists).
